title: Implement regular expression matching where '.' matches any single character and '*' matches zero or more of the preceding element, over the entire input string.
shortTitle: Regular Expression Matching: '.' and '*' with DP

s1_definition.oneliner: Star means skip two pattern chars (zero occurrences) or consume one text char if the preceding pattern char matches; dot or literal char requires a single match plus the diagonal.
s1_definition.profdef:
Regular Expression Matching uses 2D DP where dp[i][j] means the first i text chars match the first j pattern chars.

- **Star case** gives two options: zero occurrences via `dp[i][j-2]`, or one-more occurrence when the preceding pattern char matches the current text char via `dp[i-1][j]`.
- **Single match** for a literal char or dot requires `dp[i-1][j-1]` plus a character match.
- **First row** handles patterns like `a*b*` that can match empty text.
- **Time** is O(m * n) and **space** is O(m * n), reducible to O(n).
- **Full match** is required: the pattern must cover the entire text, not just a substring.
s1_definition.analogy: A reference-format validator at National Bank of India checks whether an account reference matches a pattern with wildcards. A dot matches any one character, and a star means the element before it can repeat any number of times including zero. At a star the validator tries both using none and using one more.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  DP Table for s="aab", p="c*a*b":

       ""  c  *  a  *  b
  ""  [ T  F  T  F  T  F ]
  a   [ F  F  F  T  T  F ]
  a   [ F  F  F  F  T  F ]
  b   [ F  F  F  F  F  T ]

  Star at j=2 (c*): zero c's -> dp[0][2] = dp[0][0] = T
  Star at j=4 (a*): zero a's -> dp[0][4] = dp[0][2] = T

  Star Logic:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ When pattern[j] == '*':              │
  │                                      │
  │ Option 1: Zero occurrences           │
  │   dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-2]             │
  │   (skip the x* pair entirely)        │
  │                                      │
  │ Option 2: One more occurrence        │
  │   if prev matches text[i]:           │
  │   dp[i][j] |= dp[i-1][j]            │
  │   (consume one text char, stay at *) │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Regular Expression Matching with dot and star is a two-dimensional DP problem. I define dp[i][j] as whether the first i characters of the text match the first j characters of the pattern. The empty-empty cell is true, and I handle the first row specially so that patterns like `a*` or `a*b*` can match empty text by letting each star take zero occurrences.

The body has two cases. For a normal character or dot, the cell is true only if the diagonal is true and the single character matches. For a star, there are two possibilities combined with OR: zero occurrences of the preceding element (look back two pattern positions) or one more occurrence when the preceding element matches the current text character (consume one text char and stay on the same pattern position).

The star is the whole difficulty because it modifies the preceding element rather than standing alone, which distinguishes this from Wildcard Matching where star is independent. The two classic bugs are forgetting the zero-occurrences branch and not checking that the preceding pattern character matches before allowing one-more.

In my project at National Bank of India, a validator checked whether account reference strings matched patterns with dot and star wildcards. The DP correctly handled both zero and many repetitions, which a simple left-to-right scan cannot do because it cannot backtrack.

Remember one sentence: star gives two options at each cell: skip the x-star pair for zero occurrences, or consume one text char if the preceding element matches.

---

keyPoints: dp[i][j] is true when the first i text chars match the first j pattern chars
Star gives two options: zero occurrences via dp[i][j-2], or one-more via dp[i-1][j] if preceding matches
Dot or literal char requires a single match plus the diagonal dp[i-1][j-1]
The first row handles patterns like a*b* that can match empty text
The star modifies the preceding element, unlike Wildcard Matching where star is standalone
Time and space are O(m*n), reducible to O(n) with rolling arrays
The two classic bugs: forgetting zero occurrences and not checking the preceding char match
